## Assistant

# Full credibility audit

I reviewed the scientific engines, supporting parsers and data, API implementation, documentation, and all 114 tests. I also built the complete solution, measured coverage, checked dependencies, and ran independent adversarial probes not present in the repository.

## Executive verdict

Chemy contains several correctly implemented textbook calculators and useful software components. However, the documentation systematically elevates simplified algorithms and heuristics into claims of scientific prediction, universal applicability, or industrial validation.

The appropriate classification is:

- **Credible for:** chemistry education, demonstrations, developer experiments, elementary deterministic calculations.
- **Potentially useful with validation:** reaction balancing, formula handling, simple kinetics, Hückel exercises, format generation.
- **Not credible for:** quantitative ADMET, drug safety, lead optimization, spectroscopy prediction, environmental-remediation efficiency, general thermochemistry, force-field energetics, or publication-quality molecular modelling.

The blanket claims of “industrial-grade,” “100% scientifically verified,” and a 9.5/10 credibility score are not supported.

## What was verified

- Complete solution builds successfully.
- Actual build result: **0 warnings, 0 errors**.
- Tests: **114 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped**.
- Measured core coverage:
  - Line coverage: **79.3%**
  - Branch coverage: **68.1%**
- Every major scientific source subsystem was inspected.
- Independent probes covered documented examples and failure modes.
- NuGet dependency vulnerability data was checked.

## Component-by-component findings

| Component | Does code implement the claim? | Scientific assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Periodic table | Mostly | Credible lookup table, but not a full isotope/reference system |
| Formula parser | Mostly | Good compositional parser; generated bonds are chemically unreliable |
| SMILES parser | Partially | Useful subset, not standards-compliant SMILES |
| Reaction balancing | Partially | Exact rational arithmetic for simple one-dimensional nullspaces |
| Stoichiometry | Yes, within scope | Basic mole/mass arithmetic is sound |
| Strong/weak acid pH | Mostly | Equations are sound under restricted ideal-solution assumptions |
| Buffer pH | Yes, within scope | Direct Henderson–Hasselbalch calculation |
| Electrochemistry | Yes, within scope | Correct basic Nernst calculation |
| Basic kinetics | Yes, within scope | Standard half-life and Arrhenius equations |
| Reaction networks | Mostly | RK4 is present, but “arbitrary” is overstated |
| Hückel matrix solver | Mostly | Good educational HMO implementation |
| Automatic molecular Hückel analysis | Partially | Atom typing and interpretation are heuristic |
| Thermodynamic tables | Partially | Small, phase-ambiguous lookup table |
| Benson group additivity | No, not faithfully | Loosely inspired heuristic, not a demonstrated Benson implementation |
| Molecular mechanics | No | Energy and force implementations are inconsistent |
| 3D conformers | Partially | Deterministic diagram/initial-coordinate generator, not validated conformer generation |
| TPSA/LogP/QED | No, not faithfully | Simplified approximations mislabeled as complete published methods |
| ADMET/safety | No | Threshold-generated advisory text, not predictive toxicology |
| Spectroscopy | Partially | Functional-group teaching table, not general spectral prediction |
| Graph matching | Mostly | Basic injective matcher; not VF2 or industrial substructure search |
| Ring detection | Partially | DFS cycle detection, not SSSR/Hansch ring perception |
| Lead evolution | No | Scripted mutations, not demonstrated lead optimization |
| EcoClean | No | Hard-coded narratives and manufactured efficiency values |
| Molfile/SDF export | Partially | Basic output exists; complete conformance is unproven |
| PubChem client | Mostly | Simple HTTP lookup, not particularly resilient |
| REST API | Implemented | Broad endpoint surface, but essentially untested as an API |

## Detailed evidence

### 1. Periodic table and formula calculations

The repository genuinely contains all 118 elements in frozen lookup dictionaries: [Elements.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Models/Elements.cs:126).

This supports:

- element lookup;
- atomic-number lookup;
- approximate molar-mass calculations.

It does not support the broader description of “elemental physics” or “isotopic models.” Each element has one scalar mass, and default neutron counts are obtained by rounding that mass. This is not an isotope-abundance model.

The formula parser handles nested brackets, hydrates and charges reasonably well. However, it generates molecular connectivity by connecting every atom to the first non-hydrogen atom: [FormulaParser.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Parsing/FormulaParser.cs:117).

Therefore, formula input can establish composition and mass, but generally cannot establish chemically meaningful topology, functional groups, geometry, or graph-derived properties.

### 2. SMILES parsing

The parser supports useful basic features:

- common atoms;
- branches;
- one-digit ring closures;
- single, double, triple and aromatic bonds;
- simple bracket charges and hydrogen counts.

But unsupported characters are silently ignored: [SmilesParser.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Structure/SmilesParser.cs:131).

My probes found:

- `C@C` was accepted as ethane, `C2H6`.
- `F[C@](Cl)(Br)I` and `F[C@@](Cl)(Br)I` produced indistinguishable molecular graphs.
- Stereochemistry is therefore discarded rather than merely “parsed as ordinary bonds.”

It also lacks general multi-digit ring syntax, isotope handling, robust aromatic semantics, complete bracket syntax, bond direction, and validation expected from a standards-grade SMILES implementation.

### 3. Reaction balancing

For conventional equations with a one-dimensional nullspace, the implementation genuinely uses rational Gaussian elimination and conserves charge: [MatrixSolver.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Reactions/MatrixSolver.cs:15), [Reaction.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Reactions/Reaction.cs:76).

That makes the common examples credible.

It is not, however, a general positive-integer nullspace solver. It selects only one free variable and sets other free variables to zero. My independent probe:

```text
C + O2 -> CO + CO2
```

caused a `DivideByZeroException`, although the equation admits positive balanced families. Integer overflow is also possible because rational numerators and denominators use `long`, followed by conversion to `int`.

Verdict: good basic balancer, but not universally exact.

### 4. Acid/base, electrochemistry and kinetics

These are among the strongest components.

The strong-acid equation and weak monoprotic-acid cubic are implemented as documented: [SolutionsEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Solutions/SolutionsEngine.cs:57).

Important scope limitations:

- fixed \(K_w=10^{-14}\);
- fixed `pH + pOH = 14`;
- ideal activities;
- monoprotic acids only;
- no ionic-strength or temperature dependence;
- Henderson–Hasselbalch is applied without checking its validity regime.

The Nernst implementation uses the documented constants and equation correctly: [ElectrochemistryEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Electrochemistry/ElectrochemistryEngine.cs:31).

The Arrhenius and half-life equations are also correct within their stated elementary models: [KineticsEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Kinetics/KineticsEngine.cs:55).

The general network method uses the RK4 tableau, but nonnegative clamping at intermediate and final stages changes the numerical method. The fixed cascade method lacks input validation: using zero steps returned a one-point result rather than rejecting the invalid simulation.

### 5. Thermodynamics

Hess-law arithmetic is correctly performed once appropriate formation data are available.

The weaknesses are in the data and fallback:

- The table contains only a small number of compounds.
- Phases are not represented.
- Formula aliases are used as identities.
- Isomers with the same formula receive the same properties.
- Temperature dependence of \(H\), \(S\), heat capacity and phase is absent.

For example, every `C2H6O` structure resolves to the ethanol entry, including dimethyl ether.

The claimed “true Benson group additivity” fallback begins with an invented entropy baseline:

```csharp
150 + 1.5 × R × ln(max(10, molecular weight))
```

and then applies a limited set of local increments: [ThermodynamicsEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Thermodynamics/ThermodynamicsEngine.cs:96).

This is not enough to establish a faithful, generally applicable Benson implementation. Calling it “100% universal” is contradicted by the code.

### 6. Hückel engine

The explicit-matrix pathway is one of the better scientific implementations. The Jacobi eigensolver reproduces analytical textbook eigenvalues for ethylene, butadiene, benzene and several fused systems.

Nevertheless:

- Jacobi diagonalization is numerical, not “exact.”
- The molecular atom-typing rules are limited heuristics.
- Degenerate open-shell occupancy is not handled with proper symmetry/Hund treatment.
- The UV-visible value is simply \(hc/\Delta E_{\mathrm{HOMO-LUMO}}\), not a spectral prediction with transition selection rules.
- The “Dewar resonance energy” is calculated against `number of electron pairs × 2β`, which is a simplified localized-double-bond reference.
- Multiplying benzene’s `2β` by 62.5 kcal/mol to report 125 kcal/mol should not be interpreted as an experimental aromatic stabilization energy.

Verdict: credible as an educational Hückel calculator, not general quantum chemistry or quantitative UV–Vis prediction.

### 7. Force field and 3D geometry

The force-field documentation claims the forces are the exact gradient of the implemented energy. They are not.

The energy excludes 1–2 and 1–3 nonbonded interactions: [ForceFieldEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Physics/ForceFieldEngine.cs:201).

The force calculation excludes only directly bonded 1–2 interactions: [ForceFieldEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Physics/ForceFieldEngine.cs:390).

Other discrepancies include arbitrary force scale factors and clamping. Therefore, energy and forces are mathematically inconsistent.

Additionally, the minimizer always returns:

```csharp
Converged: true
```

See [ForceFieldEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Physics/ForceFieldEngine.cs:107).

With `maxIterations = 0`, my probe returned:

- one reported iteration;
- unchanged energy;
- `Converged = true`.

The 3D system uses fixed geometries, regular polygons, breadth-first coordinate propagation and this force field. That is suitable for visualization and starting coordinates, but “physically valid conformers” and UFF/MMFF terminology are not justified.

### 8. Chemoinformatics and ADMET

The implementation does not contain the complete published Wildman–Crippen, 43-fragment Ertl TPSA, or QED algorithms.

For ibuprofen, the documentation reports:

- LogP: 4.00
- TPSA: 34.1 Å²

Actual code output was:

- LogP: **2.88**
- TPSA: **37.3 Å²**

Thus the published “live benchmark” was not generated by the current implementation: [SCIENTIFIC_VERIFICATION_BENCHMARKS.md](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/docs/SCIENTIFIC_VERIFICATION_BENCHMARKS.md:207).

Hydrogen-bond acceptors are counted as every O, N or F atom: [AdmetEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Pharmacology/AdmetEngine.cs:430). This misclassifies many standard chemical environments.

hERG, CYP and BBB output consists of fixed rules and strings, not trained or externally validated models: [AdmetEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Pharmacology/AdmetEngine.cs:80).

The system told me ibuprofen had “High BBB Permeability (CNS Active)” solely because it satisfied three thresholds. Such output should not be described as drug-safety prediction.

### 9. Spectroscopy

This is a functional-group correlation table, not a general spectrum predictor.

For acetone, documentation reports one six-proton singlet. Actual output was:

- three-proton singlet at 2.15 ppm;
- three-proton triplet at 1.15 ppm.

The code assigns a fixed three-proton ketone peak and sends remaining hydrogen to a generic aliphatic peak: [SpectroscopyEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Spectroscopy/SpectroscopyEngine.cs:143).

It does not determine chemical equivalence, coupling graphs, stereochemical relationships, solvent effects, conformational averaging, or calculated shielding/vibrational frequencies.

It is reasonable as an educational functional-group hint generator.

### 10. Lead evolution

The engine performs a small collection of scripted graph edits. It is not meaningfully a genetic or evolutionary optimization system:

- no randomized population;
- no crossover;
- no fitness-based parent selection;
- little relationship between requested generations and search depth;
- duplicate suppression is based on formula, so structural isomers collapse;
- fallback candidates duplicate the baseline while describing it as optimized.

The generated rationales make unproven claims such as eliminating hepatotoxicity, blocking CYP3A4 metabolism, increasing half-life and minimizing off-target toxicity: [MolecularEvolverEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Evolution/MolecularEvolverEngine.cs:97).

Those conclusions cannot be inferred from the implemented graph edits.

### 11. EcoClean

This is the most serious scientific credibility issue.

The engine selects predefined narrative pathways based mainly on whether particular elements or functional groups are present. It does not simulate reactions, catalysts, kinetics, yields, equilibria, competing pathways, mass balances or experimental conditions.

Efficiency is calculated as:

```csharp
99.0 + Clamp(10.0 / secondaryBde, 0.2, 0.8)
```

See [EcoCleanEngine.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Environmental/EcoCleanEngine.cs:268).

My probe returned 99.2% for PFOA. This is not a scientifically derived mineralization prediction. The test merely asserts that the result exceeds 90%: [EcoCleanTests.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core.Tests/EcoCleanTests.cs:8).

This module should be treated as speculative educational text generation, not environmental-remediation software.

### 12. Graph algorithms and file formats

The subgraph matcher is a valid small injective backtracking matcher. It is not VF2 despite that label elsewhere.

`FindRings` is DFS back-edge collection, not a demonstrated SSSR or chemically robust ring-perception algorithm: [ChemicalGraph.cs](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Core/Graph/ChemicalGraph.cs:107).

Molfile and SDF output implements basic records, but:

- formal charges are not written;
- isotope records are absent;
- V2000 size limits are not enforced;
- stereochemistry is absent;
- there is no external conformance test;
- the class description calls itself both serializer and parser, but contains no parser.

Therefore, basic interoperability is plausible; “ISO/IUPAC-compliant” and compatibility with several named products are unverified.

## Engineering and reproducibility

Positive:

- Clean build.
- Nullable reference types enabled.
- Deterministic core behavior.
- Reasonable source organization.
- Substantial unit-test coverage.

Problems:

- `TreatWarningsAsErrors` is explicitly `false`, contradicting the README: [Directory.Build.props](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Directory.Build.props:5).
- The API project suppresses `NU1903`: [Chemy.Api.csproj](/Users/moura/Desktop/chemy/src/Chemy.Api/Chemy.Api.csproj:7).
- Dependency audit found high-severity advisory `GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc` in transitive `Microsoft.OpenApi 2.0.0`.
- There are no API integration tests.
- PubChem, serialization and parts of reaction-network functionality had zero measured test coverage.
- No CI workflow was found.
- No `LICENSE` file exists despite the MIT badge.
- No `CITATION.cff`, versioned scientific dataset, benchmark-generation script, uncertainty analysis or external validation report exists.
- “Zero dependency” is false for the full product: the API uses Scalar, Swashbuckle and Microsoft OpenAPI packages.
- “Zero allocations” is false; the code uses lists, dictionaries, arrays, strings, immutable collections and records extensively.

## Final conclusion

Chemy is not fraudulent code: it contains real implementations, several sound elementary calculations, and a meaningful test suite. The problem is chiefly that its documentation does not distinguish among:

1. exact symbolic or arithmetic calculations;
2. numerical approximations;
3. empirical textbook rules;
4. visualization heuristics;
5. unsupported predictive narratives.

A scientifically defensible description would be:

> “An educational .NET chemistry toolkit providing formula parsing, common chemistry equations, basic graph operations, simplified Hückel calculations, heuristic molecular visualization, and experimental rule-based property demonstrations.”

Under that description, Chemy has credible value for students and developers. Under its current claims of industrial chemoinformatics, lead optimization, safety prediction, universal thermodynamics and environmental-remediation design, it is **not credible without substantial correction and independent validation**.

## User

ok, so what can we do, by changing code only, to close the detected gaps?

## Assistant

Code changes can close most correctness gaps, but they cannot by themselves prove scientific credibility. External datasets and independent comparison are still needed. The right approach is to make unsupported behavior impossible, then implement each model faithfully and validate it in executable tests.

## Priority 0: prevent scientifically unsafe output

Before improving models, change APIs so heuristic results cannot masquerade as measurements.

- Add metadata to every result:
  - `Method`
  - `EvidenceLevel`
  - `ApplicabilityDomain`
  - `Warnings`
  - `Uncertainty`
- Replace categorical claims such as “Low cardiac risk” or “100% mineralized” with neutral descriptors.
- Throw `NotSupportedException` when input lies outside an implementation’s supported domain.
- Never silently ignore unsupported SMILES syntax.
- Remove unconditional success/convergence flags.

A shared model could be:

```csharp
public enum EvidenceLevel
{
    ExactEquation,
    NumericalApproximation,
    EmpiricalModel,
    Heuristic
}

public record ScientificMethodInfo(
    string Method,
    string Version,
    EvidenceLevel EvidenceLevel,
    string ApplicabilityDomain,
    IReadOnlyList<string> Warnings);
```

## 1. Repair molecular identity and input handling

This is foundational because almost every higher-level engine depends on correct topology.

### Formula input

Stop generating a star-shaped bond graph from empirical formulas. A formula does not determine connectivity.

Change formula parsing to return a composition-only type:

```csharp
public record MolecularComposition(
    IReadOnlyDictionary<Element, int> ElementCounts,
    int NetCharge,
    double MolecularWeight);
```

Only topology-dependent operations should accept `Molecule`, constructed from SMILES, Molfile or explicit atoms and bonds.

### SMILES

Implement strict parsing:

- reject unknown tokens;
- preserve `@`/`@@` tetrahedral chirality;
- preserve `/` and `\` double-bond geometry;
- support `%nn` ring closures;
- parse isotope, charge and hydrogen syntax fully;
- validate ring closure, bond order and valence;
- distinguish aromatic atoms in bracket notation;
- validate disconnected components;
- return structured parse errors with positions.

Do not claim full SMILES compliance until an official or extensive public conformance corpus passes. A practical option is to expose a stable internal molecule model and use a mature chemistry toolkit for standards-compliant import.

## 2. Generalize reaction balancing

Replace the single-free-variable solver with a complete rational nullspace-basis calculation.

Required behavior:

1. Compute every free-variable basis vector.
2. Find a strictly positive integer combination of basis vectors.
3. Minimize the resulting coefficient vector.
4. Detect:
   - no solution;
   - unique primitive solution;
   - multiple valid solutions;
   - species requiring zero coefficients.
5. Use `BigInteger` instead of `long` and `int`.
6. Verify the final vector by multiplying it back into the conservation matrix.

For underdetermined reactions, return ambiguity explicitly:

```csharp
public record BalanceResult(
    BalanceStatus Status,
    IReadOnlyList<BigInteger>? Coefficients,
    int Nullity,
    string? Explanation);
```

Add adversarial tests for underdetermined equations, ionic equations, duplicated species, impossible equations, large coefficients and overflow cases.

## 3. Correct numerical chemistry engines

### Acid/base

Make equilibrium conditions explicit:

- configurable temperature and \(K_w(T)\);
- activity coefficients or an explicit ideal-solution flag;
- strong bases;
- weak bases;
- polyprotic acids;
- buffer charge balance instead of unconditional Henderson–Hasselbalch;
- convergence status, residual and iteration count;
- safeguards for Halley denominator failure or negative iterates.

Return numerical diagnostics:

```csharp
public record EquilibriumResult(
    double Ph,
    double Residual,
    int Iterations,
    bool Converged,
    IReadOnlyList<string> Assumptions);
```

### Reaction networks

- Validate all concentrations, rates, time and step counts.
- Verify rate-law output length and finite values.
- Remove intermediate nonnegative clamping from nominal RK4.
- Make positivity preservation an explicit solver option.
- Add adaptive RK45 with error tolerances.
- Report rejected steps and conservation residuals.
- Compare against analytical solutions for first-order networks.

### Electrochemistry

The equation is already fundamentally sound. Add:

- strictly positive temperature;
- activity-based terminology;
- unit-aware inputs;
- uncertainty propagation where inputs include uncertainty;
- tests at several temperatures and limiting values.

## 4. Rebuild the force field coherently

This requires more than patching one exclusion.

### Mathematical correctness

- Derive every force from exactly the same energy expression.
- Remove arbitrary `0.001` and `0.0005` multipliers.
- Apply identical 1–2, 1–3 and optional scaled 1–4 handling in energy and gradients.
- Do not clamp individual forces unless using an explicitly documented stabilization mode.
- Preserve signed total potential energy; do not force it to be nonnegative.
- Use element- and atom-type-specific parameters.
- Handle electrostatics explicitly or state that the model omits them.

### Minimization

- Set `Converged` only when a real criterion passes.
- Return `MaximumIterationsReached`, `NumericalFailure` or `LineSearchFailed`.
- Track gradient norm, energy change and step size.
- Reject `maxIterations <= 0`.
- Use a proper optimizer such as L-BFGS or nonlinear conjugate gradient with line search.

### Verification

For every energy term, compare analytical and central finite-difference gradients:

```text
|F_analytical + dE/dx_finite-difference| < tolerance
```

Test translation/rotation invariance, permutation invariance, known equilibrium geometries and energy decrease during accepted optimization steps.

Until parameterized against an actual published force field, call it a “toy molecular-mechanics potential,” not UFF or MMFF.

## 5. Separate coordinate drawing from conformer generation

Create distinct APIs:

- `GenerateVseprGeometry`
- `Generate2DLayout`
- `GenerateInitial3DCoordinates`
- `GenerateConformers`

A real conformer generator needs:

- stereochemical constraints;
- distance-geometry embedding;
- ring templates;
- multiple starting conformers;
- torsion sampling;
- force-field minimization;
- RMSD deduplication;
- energy ranking;
- deterministic seed support.

A visual layout must not be returned as a physically meaningful conformer.

## 6. Implement descriptors faithfully

### TPSA

Replace the current decision tree with the complete published atom-fragment table.

- Define explicit atom types.
- Assign exactly one applicable fragment to every relevant atom.
- Return an error or warning for untyped atoms.
- Add a public atom-contribution breakdown.
- Test hundreds of structures against a trusted implementation.

### Wildman–Crippen LogP

Implement the complete atom-type and correction system rather than approximate element contributions.

Return:

```csharp
public record AtomContribution(
    int AtomIndex,
    string AtomType,
    double Contribution);
```

### Hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors

Use environment-sensitive rules:

- exclude amide and sulfonamide nitrogen as acceptors;
- distinguish pyridine and pyrrole;
- handle protonated/quaternary nitrogen;
- handle acidic hydroxyls;
- do not treat organic fluorine as a general acceptor;
- account for formal charge and resonance.

### Rotatable bonds and rings

Define the precise convention being implemented. Exclude amide C–N bonds and terminal-heavy-atom bonds as required by that convention. Replace DFS ring counting with a chemically defined cycle/ring algorithm.

### QED

Implement the original ADS equations and published coefficients exactly. Do not reuse a single simplified logistic shape for every descriptor. Validate final QED values against a reference set.

## 7. Remove predictive ADMET claims or introduce real models

Descriptor rules cannot produce credible hERG, CYP, BBB or toxicity predictions.

Two code-only options exist:

### Safe short-term option

Remove those fields and return only measured descriptors and explicit rule evaluations:

```csharp
LipinskiResult
VeberResult
GhoseResult
DescriptorProfile
```

### Long-term modelling option

Implement versioned models with:

- serialized model parameters;
- defined descriptor vectors;
- applicability-domain calculation;
- probability rather than categorical prose;
- calibration;
- missing-feature handling;
- uncertainty/confidence intervals;
- model provenance and training-dataset hash.

Even then, external validation remains necessary.

## 8. Reclassify spectroscopy as functional-group hints

Short term:

- Rename `SpectroscopyPrediction` to `SpectralFeatureHints`.
- Do not allocate hydrogen/carbon counts using generic remainder logic.
- Return ranges rather than artificial exact peaks.
- Stop predicting splitting unless neighbor equivalence and coupling are actually analysed.
- Avoid claiming complete spectra.

A more serious implementation would require:

- graph-based proton/carbon environment canonicalization;
- symmetry-equivalence detection;
- diastereotopic proton handling;
- \(n+1\) coupling based on actual adjacent nuclei;
- substituent increments;
- solvent/reference metadata;
- vibrational mode or validated group-frequency modelling.

First fix the acetone regression so it produces one six-proton environment.

## 9. Replace scripted “evolution” with a valid search engine

At minimum:

- represent candidates by canonical structural identity, not formula;
- validate valence after every mutation;
- preserve stereochemistry;
- ensure returned SMILES describes the returned molecular graph;
- remove duplicate fallback candidates;
- make mutations chemically localized and reversible;
- score only descriptors that are actually implemented;
- never assert improved toxicity, metabolism or binding without a model.

For a genuine evolutionary algorithm, add:

- population initialization;
- configurable mutation probabilities;
- selection;
- crossover, if chemically meaningful;
- elitism;
- diversity constraints;
- deterministic random seed;
- generation history;
- constraint rejection;
- Pareto ranking instead of a single unvalidated score.

It should produce “enumerated candidates,” not “optimized leads,” unless biological activity is part of the objective.

## 10. Replace EcoClean with a knowledge/rule system

Delete computed efficiency and half-life outputs until supported by real models.

A defensible replacement could return:

```csharp
public record DegradationHypothesis(
    string Transformation,
    IReadOnlyList<string> RequiredConditions,
    IReadOnlyList<string> PossibleProducts,
    EvidenceLevel EvidenceLevel,
    IReadOnlyList<string> Limitations);
```

If quantitative modelling is desired, it needs explicit:

- reaction stoichiometry;
- kinetic rate laws;
- catalyst and concentration parameters;
- temperature, pH and medium;
- competing reactions;
- mass-balance verification;
- uncertainty;
- experimentally fitted parameters.

Never generate “100% mineralized” merely from the elements present.

## 11. Improve Hückel boundaries

Keep the explicit-matrix solver; it is useful.

Change the molecular analysis to:

- use robust conjugated-component detection;
- analyse disconnected conjugated systems separately;
- define atom parameters in a versioned table;
- reject unparameterized environments;
- handle charge and radical electron counts;
- deal correctly with degenerate open-shell occupancy;
- report numerical eigensolver residuals;
- call it numerical Jacobi diagonalization, not exact diagonalization.

Rename UV–Vis output to something like `OrbitalGapEquivalentWavelength`. It must not imply that transition intensity, selection rules or excited-state relaxation were calculated.

## 12. Strengthen formats and API behavior

### Chemical formats

- Write formal charges through `M  CHG`.
- Write isotopes through `M  ISO`.
- enforce V2000 atom/bond limits;
- preserve stereochemical bond flags;
- validate coordinates and indices;
- add round-trip parsers;
- test generated files with independent readers;
- distinguish 2D and 3D header flags correctly.

### API

- Add integration tests for every endpoint.
- Use one health endpoint rather than overlapping middleware and route mappings.
- Add request-size and complexity limits for parsers and graph algorithms.
- Add cancellation support for expensive operations.
- Stop returning exception internals as public error messages.
- Introduce consistent problem-details responses.
- Remove broad `AllowAnyOrigin` as the unconditional production default.
- Add OpenAPI schemas describing assumptions and evidence levels.

### Dependencies

- Upgrade the dependency chain that currently resolves vulnerable `Microsoft.OpenApi 2.0.0`.
- Remove the `NU1903` suppression.
- Enable:

```xml
<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
<NuGetAudit>true</NuGetAudit>
<NuGetAuditMode>all</NuGetAuditMode>
```

## Recommended implementation order

1. Strict molecular input model and separation of composition from topology.
2. Remove unsafe ADMET/EcoClean/lead-optimization conclusions.
3. Repair force-field energy, gradients and convergence.
4. Generalize reaction nullspace solving.
5. Implement faithful TPSA, LogP, HBD/HBA and QED.
6. Add numerical diagnostics to equilibria and kinetics.
7. Separate diagram generation from conformer generation.
8. Correct thermodynamic identity, phase and applicability handling.
9. Reclassify or rebuild spectroscopy.
10. Harden formats, API, dependencies and integration tests.
11. Add executable reference datasets and differential tests.

The most important architectural rule is: **if the code cannot calculate a property defensibly, return “unsupported” rather than manufacture a confident answer.** That change alone would eliminate the most serious credibility failures.

## Proposed PR

**Title**

`fix: enforce scientific validity boundaries and numerical correctness`

**Purpose**

Prevent Chemy from reporting unsupported scientific conclusions, fix confirmed force-field and solver defects, reject silently misparsed inputs, and expose method limitations programmatically.

### Changes

1. **Scientific result metadata**
   - Add `ScientificMethodInfo`, `EvidenceLevel`, warnings, applicability domain, and convergence diagnostics.
   - Attach metadata to ADMET, EcoClean, force-field, spectroscopy, thermodynamics, and equilibrium results.

2. **Force-field correctness**
   - Use identical 1–2 and 1–3 exclusions for energy and gradients.
   - Remove arbitrary gradient scale factors.
   - Stop clamping total energy to zero.
   - Report genuine convergence status and termination reason.
   - Reject nonpositive iteration limits.
   - Add finite-difference gradient tests.

3. **Strict input handling**
   - Reject unsupported SMILES tokens such as `@`, `@@`, `/`, and `\` until they are actually implemented.
   - Reject unmatched branches and ring closures.
   - Stop silently ignoring unknown characters.
   - Mark formula-derived molecules as composition-only and reject topology-dependent operations on them.

4. **Reaction balancing**
   - Prevent the underdetermined-nullspace crash.
   - Return an explicit `Ambiguous` or `Unsupported` result when more than one free variable exists.
   - Verify every computed coefficient vector against the original conservation matrix.
   - Introduce `BigInteger` rational arithmetic to prevent overflow.

5. **Remove unsupported predictions**
   - Replace hERG, CYP and BBB classifications with descriptor-only rule results.
   - Remove computed EcoClean efficiency, environmental half-life, “non-toxic,” and “100% mineralized” outputs.
   - Rename spectroscopy results to `SpectralFeatureHints`.
   - Rename evolved leads to `EnumeratedCandidate`.
   - Remove claims that mutations improve toxicity, metabolism, binding or bioavailability.

6. **API and dependency hardening**
   - Upgrade the vulnerable `Microsoft.OpenApi` dependency chain.
   - Remove `NU1903` suppression.
   - Enable warnings as errors and NuGet auditing.
   - Return standardized problem details.
   - Add request validation and API integration tests.
   - Resolve the overlapping `/healthz` registrations.

### Expected breaking changes

- ADMET, EcoClean, spectroscopy and evolution response schemas change.
- Unsupported SMILES constructs now return errors.
- Formula inputs can no longer be used for graph-dependent analysis.
- Force-field minimization may report non-convergence.
- Ambiguous reaction equations no longer throw an internal exception.
- Some existing benchmark snapshots must be replaced because they do not match actual code output.

## Draft PR description

```markdown
## Summary

This PR establishes explicit scientific-validity boundaries across Chemy and
fixes confirmed numerical and input-handling defects.

It does not attempt to turn heuristic components into validated predictive
models. Instead, unsupported conclusions are removed or identified as
heuristics, invalid inputs are rejected, and numerical algorithms report
honest convergence and applicability information.

## Fixed defects

- Align force-field energy and gradient nonbonded exclusions.
- Report actual minimizer convergence and termination reason.
- Reject nonpositive optimization limits.
- Reject unsupported SMILES syntax instead of silently discarding it.
- Prevent underdetermined reaction balancing from crashing.
- Verify balanced coefficient vectors.
- Remove manufactured PFAS efficiency and half-life values.
- Remove rule-generated clinical safety classifications.
- Distinguish spectral hints from spectrum prediction.
- Remove vulnerable OpenAPI dependency and NU1903 suppression.

## Breaking changes

- Several scientific result DTOs now contain method metadata and warnings.
- ADMET, EcoClean, spectroscopy, and molecular-evolution schemas have changed.
- Formula-only inputs are rejected by topology-dependent endpoints.
- Unsupported SMILES stereochemistry returns a structured parse error.

## Validation

- Full solution builds with warnings treated as errors.
- Existing applicable unit tests pass.
- Regression tests cover every corrected audit finding.
- Force-field gradients are checked independently using central differences.
- API endpoints have integration coverage.
- NuGet audit reports no known high-severity vulnerabilities.

## Out of scope

Faithful implementations of full Ertl TPSA, Wildman–Crippen LogP, published
QED, Benson group additivity, conformer generation, and predictive ADMET.
These will be delivered as separate independently reviewable PRs.
```

    +    // Central differences deliberately derive forces from the same energy function.
    +    // This is slower than a closed-form gradient but guarantees mathematical consistency
    +    // while the generalized potential remains small and educational in scope.
         private static List<Vector3D> CalculateGradients(Molecule3D molecule3D, List<Vector3D> positions)
         {
    +        const double delta = 1e-5;
    +        var forces = new List<Vector3D>(positions.Count);
    +
    +        for (int atom = 0; atom < positions.Count; atom++)
    +        {
    +            double fx = -CentralDerivative(molecule3D, positions, atom, 0, delta);
    +            double fy = -CentralDerivative(molecule3D, positions, atom, 1, delta);
    +            double fz = -CentralDerivative(molecule3D, positions, atom, 2, delta);
    +            forces.Add(new Vector3D(fx, fy, fz));
    +        }
    +
    +        return forces;
    +    }
    +
    +    private static double CentralDerivative(Molecule3D molecule3D, List<Vector3D> positions, int atom, int axis, double delta)
    +    {
    +        var original = positions[atom];
    +        positions[atom] = axis switch
    +        {
    +            0 => original with { X = original.X + delta },
    +            1 => original with { Y = original.Y + delta },
    +            _ => original with { Z = original.Z + delta }
    +        };
    +        double plus = CalculateTotalPotentialEnergy(molecule3D, positions);
    +
    +        positions[atom] = axis switch
    +        {
    +            0 => original with { X = original.X - delta },
    +            1 => original with { Y = original.Y - delta },
    +            _ => original with { Z = original.Z - delta }
    +        };
    +        double minus = CalculateTotalPotentialEnergy(molecule3D, positions);
    +        positions[atom] = original;
    +        return (plus - minus) / (2.0 * delta);
    +    }

    +    {

    +            .Where(b => b.Type == BondType.Double)

      using System.Collections.Immutable;
      using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis;
      using System.Text;
      using Chemy.Core.Parsing;
      using Chemy.Core.Quantum;
      using Chemy.Core.Rendering;
      using Chemy.Core.Spatial;
      using Chemy.Core.Structure;
      
      namespace Chemy.Core;
      
      /// <summary>
      /// Immutable molecular entity encapsulating an atomic graph, covalent bonding topology,
      /// Hill-system empirical formula, molar mass, and net electrical charge.
      /// </summary>
      public record Molecule
      {
          /// <summary>Common or IUPAC name of the molecule.</summary>
          public string Name { get; init; }
      
          /// <summary>Immutable list of constituent atoms comprising the molecule.</summary>
          public ImmutableList<Atom> Atoms { get; init; }
      
          /// <summary>Immutable list of covalent/ionic/aromatic bonds connecting atom indices.</summary>
          public ImmutableList<Bond> Bonds { get; init; }
      
          /// <summary>Molar mass calculated from standard IUPAC atomic weights (in g/mol or u).</summary>
          public double MolecularWeight => Atoms.Sum(a => a.Element.StandardAtomicMass);
      
          /// <summary>Net electrostatic charge computed from the sum of atomic net charges.</summary>
          public int NetCharge => Atoms.Sum(a => a.NetCharge);
      
          /// <summary>
          /// Constructs a Molecule instance with validated bonding graph topology.
          /// </summary>
          /// <param name="name">Descriptive name.</param>
          /// <param name="atoms">Collection of constituent atoms.</param>
          /// <param name="bonds">Optional collection of chemical bonds between atoms.</param>
          public Molecule(string name, IEnumerable<Atom> atoms, IEnumerable<Bond>? bonds = null)
          {
              ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(name);
              ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(atoms);
      
              Name = name;
              Atoms = atoms.ToImmutableList();
              Bonds = (bonds ?? Enumerable.Empty<Bond>()).ToImmutableList();
      
              ValidateBonds();
          }
      
          /// <summary>
          /// Ensures that all bond indices map to valid atoms and no self-loops exist.
          /// </summary>
          private void ValidateBonds()
          {
              int count = Atoms.Count;
              foreach (var bond in Bonds)
              {
                  if (bond.Atom1Index < 0 || bond.Atom1Index >= count || bond.Atom2Index < 0 || bond.Atom2Index >= count)
                  {
                      throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(Bonds), $"Bond indices ({bond.Atom1Index}, {bond.Atom2Index}) are out of range for atom count {count}.");
                  }
      
                  if (bond.Atom1Index == bond.Atom2Index)
                  {
                      throw new ArgumentException($"Self-referencing bond at atom index {bond.Atom1Index} is invalid.");
                  }
              }
          }
      
          /// <summary>
          /// Formats the empirical chemical formula following the IUPAC Hill system
          /// (Carbon first, Hydrogen second, followed by all remaining elements in alphabetical order).
          /// </summary>
          public string ChemicalFormula
          {
              get
              {
                  var counts = Atoms
                      .GroupBy(a => a.Element.Symbol)
                      .ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count());
      
                  var builder = new StringBuilder();
      
                  // Hill system: C first, then H
                  if (counts.Remove("C", out int cCount))
                  {
                      AppendElement(builder, "C", cCount);
                      if (counts.Remove("H", out int hCount))
                      {
                          AppendElement(builder, "H", hCount);
                      }
                  }

    # Chemy Scientific Credibility Audit
    
    > **Audit snapshot:** This report describes the repository before the scientific-validity changes in commit `b436fe3` (`fix: enforce scientific validity boundaries`). Some findings have since been addressed on the `fix/scientific-validity-boundaries` branch. The report is retained as the baseline assessment that motivated those changes.
    
    ## Executive verdict
    
    Chemy contains several correctly implemented textbook calculators and useful software components. However, its documentation systematically elevates simplified algorithms and heuristics into claims of scientific prediction, universal applicability, or industrial validation.
    
    The appropriate classification at the time of this audit was:
    
    - **Credible for:** chemistry education, demonstrations, developer experiments, and elementary deterministic calculations.
    - **Potentially useful with validation:** reaction balancing, formula handling, simple kinetics, Hückel exercises, and chemical-format generation.
    - **Not credible for:** quantitative ADMET, drug safety, lead optimization, spectroscopy prediction, environmental-remediation efficiency, general thermochemistry, force-field energetics, or publication-quality molecular modelling.
    
    The blanket claims of “industrial-grade,” “100% scientifically verified,” and a 9.5/10 credibility score were not supported by the repository evidence.
    
    ## Audit method
    
    The assessment included:
    
    - inspection of every major scientific subsystem;
    - comparison of implementation behavior with README and scientific-documentation claims;
    - inspection of all 114 tests;
    - a complete solution build and test run;
    - code-coverage measurement;
    - dependency vulnerability inspection;
    - independent adversarial probes not authored by the project.
    
    At the time of the audit:
    
    - the solution built with 0 warnings and 0 errors;
    - 114 tests passed, with no failures or skips;
    - core line coverage was approximately 79.3%;
    - core branch coverage was approximately 68.1%.
    
    Passing tests supported regression stability, but did not establish scientific validity for every advertised domain.
    
    ## Component summary
    
    | Component | Did code implement the claim? | Assessment |
    |---|---|---|
    | Periodic table | Mostly | Credible lookup table, but not a complete isotope/reference system |
    | Formula parser | Mostly | Good compositional parser; generated bonds were chemically unreliable |
    | SMILES parser | Partially | Useful subset, not standards-compliant SMILES |
    | Reaction balancing | Partially | Exact rational arithmetic for simple one-dimensional nullspaces |
    | Stoichiometry | Yes, within scope | Basic mole/mass arithmetic was sound |
    | Strong/weak acid pH | Mostly | Sound equations under restricted ideal-solution assumptions |
    | Buffer pH | Yes, within scope | Direct Henderson–Hasselbalch calculation |
    | Electrochemistry | Yes, within scope | Correct basic Nernst calculation |
    | Basic kinetics | Yes, within scope | Standard half-life and Arrhenius equations |
    | Reaction networks | Mostly | RK4 was present, but “arbitrary” was overstated |
    | Hückel matrix solver | Mostly | Useful educational HMO implementation |
    | Automatic molecular Hückel analysis | Partially | Atom typing and interpretation were heuristic |
    | Thermodynamic tables | Partially | Small, phase-ambiguous lookup table |
    | Benson group additivity | No, not faithfully | Loosely inspired heuristic, not a demonstrated Benson implementation |
    | Molecular mechanics | No | Energy and force implementations were inconsistent |
    | 3D conformers | Partially | Diagram/initial-coordinate generator, not validated conformer generation |
    | TPSA/LogP/QED | No, not faithfully | Simplified approximations labeled as complete published methods |
    | ADMET/safety | No | Threshold-generated advisory text, not predictive toxicology |
    | Spectroscopy | Partially | Functional-group teaching table, not general spectral prediction |
    | Graph matching | Mostly | Basic injective matcher; not VF2 or industrial substructure search |
    | Ring detection | Partially | DFS cycle detection, not SSSR/Hansch ring perception |
    | Lead evolution | No | Scripted mutations, not demonstrated lead optimization |
    | EcoClean | No | Hard-coded narratives and manufactured efficiency values |
    | Molfile/SDF export | Partially | Basic output existed; complete conformance was unproven |
    | PubChem client | Mostly | Simple HTTP lookup, not a resilient integration |
    | REST API | Implemented | Broad endpoint surface, but essentially untested as an API |
    
    ## Detailed findings
    
    ### 1. Periodic table and formula calculations
    
    The repository contained all 118 elements in frozen lookup dictionaries. This supported element lookup, atomic-number lookup, and approximate molar-mass calculations.
    
    It did not support the broader description of “elemental physics” or “isotopic models.” Each element had one scalar mass, and default neutron counts were obtained by rounding that mass. This was not an isotope-abundance model.
    
    The formula parser handled nested brackets, hydrates, and charges reasonably well. However, it generated molecular connectivity by connecting every atom to the first non-hydrogen atom. Formula input could therefore establish composition and mass, but generally could not establish chemically meaningful topology, functional groups, geometry, or graph-derived properties.
    
    ### 2. SMILES parsing
    
    The parser supported common atoms, branches, one-digit ring closures, common bond orders, aromatic bonds, and simple bracket charges and hydrogen counts.
    
    Unsupported characters were silently ignored. Independent probes found:
    
    - `C@C` was accepted as ethane, `C2H6`;
    - `F[C@](Cl)(Br)I` and `F[C@@](Cl)(Br)I` produced indistinguishable graphs;
    - stereochemistry was discarded rather than preserved.
    
    The parser also lacked general multi-digit ring syntax, isotope handling, robust aromatic semantics, complete bracket syntax, bond direction, and validation expected from a standards-grade implementation.
    
    ### 3. Reaction balancing
    
    For conventional equations with a one-dimensional nullspace, the implementation genuinely used rational Gaussian elimination and conserved charge. The common documented examples were credible.
    
    It was not a general positive-integer nullspace solver. It selected one free variable and left other free variables at zero. The independent probe:
    
    ```text
    C + O2 -> CO + CO2
    ```
    
    caused a `DivideByZeroException`, although the equation admits positive balanced families. Integer overflow was also possible because rational values used `long` before conversion to `int`.
    
    ### 4. Acid/base, electrochemistry, and kinetics
    
    These were among the strongest components.
    
    The documented strong-acid equation and weak-monoprotic-acid cubic were implemented. Their applicability was nevertheless limited by:
    
    - fixed `Kw = 1e-14`;
    - fixed `pH + pOH = 14`;
    - ideal activities;
    - monoprotic acids only;
    - no ionic-strength or temperature dependence;
    - unconditional Henderson–Hasselbalch use without a validity check.
    
    The Nernst implementation used the documented constants and equation correctly. Arrhenius and standard half-life equations were also correct within their elementary models.
    
    The general reaction-network method used the RK4 tableau, but nonnegative clamping at intermediate and final stages changed the numerical method. The fixed cascade method did not validate all inputs: a zero-step simulation returned a one-point result rather than rejecting the request.
    
    ### 5. Thermodynamics
    
    Hess-law arithmetic was correctly performed once appropriate formation data were available.
    
    The limitations were primarily in identity, reference data, and fallback estimation:
    
    - only a small compound table was present;
    - physical phases were not represented;
    - formulas and aliases were used as compound identities;
    - isomers with the same formula received the same properties;
    - heat-capacity, temperature, and phase-transition effects were absent.
    
    For example, every `C2H6O` structure resolved to the ethanol entry, including dimethyl ether.
    
    The claimed “true Benson group additivity” fallback began with an ad hoc entropy baseline based on molecular weight and applied a limited set of local increments. This did not establish a faithful, generally applicable Benson implementation. Calling the engine “100% universal” was contradicted by the code.
    
    ### 6. Hückel engine
    
    The explicit-matrix pathway was one of the stronger scientific implementations. The Jacobi eigensolver reproduced analytical textbook eigenvalues for ethylene, butadiene, benzene, and several fused systems.
    
    Important limitations remained:
    
    - Jacobi diagonalization is numerical, not exact;
    - automatic molecular atom typing used limited heuristics;
    - degenerate open-shell occupancy was not treated rigorously;
    - UV-visible output was simply `hc / HOMO-LUMO gap`, without transition selection rules or intensities;
    - the resonance calculation used a simplified localized-double-bond reference;
    - the reported benzene value of 125 kcal/mol should not be interpreted as experimental aromatic stabilization energy.
    
    The engine was credible as an educational Hückel calculator, not as general quantum chemistry or quantitative UV-visible prediction.
    
    ### 7. Force field and 3D geometry
    
    The documentation claimed that the forces were the exact analytical gradient of the implemented energy. They were not.
    
    The energy excluded 1–2 and 1–3 nonbonded interactions, whereas the force calculation excluded only directly bonded 1–2 interactions. Additional arbitrary scale factors and force clamping made the energy and force implementations mathematically inconsistent.
    
    The minimizer also returned `Converged = true` unconditionally. With `maxIterations = 0`, an independent probe reported one iteration, unchanged energy, and successful convergence.
    
    The 3D system used fixed geometries, regular polygons, breadth-first coordinate propagation, and this generalized force field. That was useful for visualization and starting coordinates, but did not justify claims of physically valid conformers or UFF/MMFF behavior.
    
    ### 8. Chemoinformatics and ADMET
    
    The code did not contain complete implementations of the published Wildman–Crippen, 43-fragment Ertl TPSA, or QED algorithms.
    
    For ibuprofen, the documentation reported:
    
    - LogP: 4.00;
    - TPSA: 34.1 Å².
    
    The audited implementation returned:
    
    - LogP: 2.88;
    - TPSA: 37.3 Å².
    
    The published “live benchmark” therefore did not match the current implementation.
    
    Hydrogen-bond acceptors were counted as every oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine atom. That misclassified amide nitrogen, protonated and pyrrolic nitrogen, acidic groups, and covalently bound fluorine.
    
    hERG, CYP, and blood-brain-barrier output consisted of fixed thresholds and prose, not trained or externally validated models. An audit probe classified ibuprofen as having “High BBB Permeability (CNS Active)” solely because it passed three descriptor thresholds. This was not a defensible drug-safety prediction.
    
    ### 9. Spectroscopy
    
    The spectroscopy engine was a functional-group correlation table, not a general spectrum predictor.
    
    For acetone, documentation reported one six-proton singlet. The implementation returned:
    
    - a three-proton singlet at 2.15 ppm;
    - a three-proton triplet at 1.15 ppm.
    
    The engine did not determine chemical equivalence, coupling graphs, stereochemical relationships, solvent effects, conformational averaging, or calculated shielding and vibrational frequencies. It was reasonable as an educational functional-group hint generator.
    
    ### 10. Lead evolution
    
    The engine performed a small set of scripted graph edits. It was not meaningfully a genetic or evolutionary optimization system:
    
    - no randomized population;
    - no crossover;
    - no fitness-based parent selection;
    - little relationship between requested generations and search depth;
    - duplicate suppression based on formula rather than molecular identity;
    - duplicate baseline fallbacks described as optimized candidates.
    
    Generated rationales claimed improvements in toxicity, metabolism, binding, half-life, and bioavailability that could not be inferred from the implemented graph edits.
    
    ### 11. EcoClean
    
    EcoClean was the most serious scientific-credibility issue found.
    
    The engine selected predefined narrative pathways based mainly on the elements and functional groups present. It did not simulate reactions, catalysts, kinetics, yields, equilibria, competing pathways, experimental conditions, or mass balance.
    
    Mineralization efficiency was generated from:
    
    ```csharp
    99.0 + Math.Clamp(10.0 / secondaryBde, 0.2, 0.8)
    ```
    
    An independent PFOA probe returned 99.2%. This was not a scientifically derived mineralization prediction. The dedicated test merely asserted that the result exceeded 90%, confirming the hard-coded behavior rather than validating it.
    
    ### 12. Graph algorithms and chemical formats
    
    The subgraph matcher was a valid small injective backtracking matcher, but was not VF2 despite that label appearing elsewhere.
    
    Ring detection used DFS back-edge collection rather than a demonstrated SSSR or chemically robust ring-perception algorithm.
    
    Molfile and SDF output implemented basic records. However:
    
    - formal charges were not written;
    - isotope records were absent;
    - V2000 size limits were not enforced;
    - stereochemistry was absent;
    - external conformance tests were absent;
    - the exporter was described as a parser despite containing no parser.
    
    Basic interoperability was plausible, but complete standards compliance and compatibility with named third-party applications were unverified.
    
    ## Engineering and reproducibility findings
    
    Positive findings included:
    
    - clean compilation;
    - nullable reference types;
    - deterministic core behavior;
    - reasonable project organization;
    - meaningful unit-test coverage.
    
    Problems included:
    
    - `TreatWarningsAsErrors` was explicitly `false` despite the README claiming enforcement;
    - the API suppressed `NU1903`;
    - the dependency graph contained high-severity advisory `GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc` through `Microsoft.OpenApi 2.0.0`;
    - API integration tests were absent;
    - PubChem, serialization, and parts of reaction-network functionality had no measured coverage;
    - no CI workflow was present;
    - no `LICENSE` file existed despite an MIT badge;
    - no `CITATION.cff`, versioned scientific dataset, benchmark-generation script, uncertainty analysis, or independent validation report was present;
    - “zero dependency” was false for the full product;
    - “zero allocations” was contradicted throughout the implementation.
    
    ## Conclusion
    
    Chemy was not empty or fraudulent software. It contained genuine implementations, several sound elementary calculations, and a meaningful regression suite. Its central credibility problem was failure to distinguish between:
    
    1. exact arithmetic and textbook equations;
    2. numerical approximations;
    3. empirical models;
    4. visualization and classification heuristics;
    5. unsupported predictive narratives.
    
    A defensible description of the audited code was:
    
    > An educational .NET chemistry toolkit providing formula parsing, common chemistry equations, basic graph operations, simplified Hückel calculations, heuristic molecular visualization, and experimental rule-based property demonstrations.
    
    Under that description, Chemy had credible value for students and developers. Under its advertised claims of industrial chemoinformatics, lead optimization, safety prediction, universal thermodynamics, and environmental-remediation design, it was not credible without substantial correction and independent validation.
    
    ## Remediation boundary
    
    Code changes can correct mathematical defects, reject unsupported inputs, expose applicability information, and remove manufactured predictions. Code alone cannot establish experimental validity. Credible scientific claims ultimately require versioned reference datasets, reproducible benchmark generation, error metrics, applicability-domain analysis, and independent comparison or review.
